messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 29-year-old jeweler, presented for treatment six months after returning from a volunteer stint as a relief worker in a conflict zone. The man who sat in the office was a shadow of the person his friends described from before he left: gaunt, jumpy, with a pervasive tension that seemed to hold his entire body rigid. He spoke of a constant, humming anxiety that had dismantled his life piece by piece, starting with the work he once loved. The fine, steady hands required to set a gemstone now trembled, and the quiet focus of his workshop had become a place of profound threat.

The trauma occurred during a chaotic food distribution at a makeshift camp. David was handing out supplies to a crowd of displaced families when a mortar strike hit the perimeter. The blast was disorienting, but it was the aftermath that broke him. Amid the screaming and dust, he remembers the piercing sound of children crying, a sound that seemed to come from every direction at once. As people scrambled for cover, someone grabbed him hard and unexpectedly from behind, pulling him to the ground. He lay there, his heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he was about to die, the wails of terrified children the only thing he could hear. That memory now feels more real and vivid to him than what he had for breakfast. Because the memory feels so immediate and unresolved, the elements within it—the sound of crying, the feeling of his own heart racing—have become powerful triggers in his daily life, each one a sign that the danger is not over.

His pervasive sense of threat has become the organizing principle of his life. At his jeweler’s bench, he finds himself constantly scanning his small showroom, cataloging how the heavy mallet could be a weapon, or how the sharp point of a graver could be used to harm. This hypervigilance means he cannot trust that he is safe, even when the door is locked. This constant state of alert also primes his memory; any sudden noise or movement can feel like a precursor to attack, instantly pulling the chaos of the camp into the present moment. This feeling is so powerful that when a client recently reached out to pat his shoulder in thanks, the unexpected touch sent a jolt of pure terror through him, bringing with it the phantom sensation of being dragged to the ground.

These triggers are everywhere. The sound of a child crying in the grocery store is enough to bring the memory back in a full, sensory rush, without warning. His own heart racing after climbing the stairs to his apartment becomes, in his mind, not a sign of exertion but a prelude to imminent death, mirroring the terror he felt lying in the dust. This physiological echo often brings back the memory with such force that he has to brace himself against a wall. Sometimes, there is no clear image, just the raw, unfiltered emotion of the event—a wave of horror and helplessness that leaves him gasping for air.

In the face of these overwhelming experiences, David has developed a set of rigid coping rules. When a memory surfaces, he immediately fights it, forcing himself to think of something, anything, positive. He repeats mantras about the beauty of a particular gemstone or the quiet of his apartment. He tells himself it could have been much worse, that he was lucky to get out alive. These attempts to suppress the memory are his primary defense, alongside a relentless, moment-to-moment scan of his surroundings for any sign of danger, his back always to a wall so he can see every entrance.

These strategies, however, have become a cage. The constant scanning only reinforces his deeply held belief that the world is a dangerous place and that he is never truly safe. His efforts to force positive thoughts and remind himself it could have been worse do not process the trauma; they simply push it down, ensuring it will erupt again later with even greater intensity. This constant suppression has made him exquisitely sensitive to his triggers. By trying so hard not to think about the crying, he hears it everywhere. By monitoring his own body for signs of panic, his own heartbeat has become a source of terror. His attempts to control his experience are, in fact, what keep the trauma alive, fueling a self-reinforcing cycle of threat, intrusion, and failed coping that has slowly strangled his world. He came to therapy after dropping and shattering a valuable diamond, his hands shaking too violently to work, finally admitting that his strategies were not saving him but burying him.
